board-squares.prompt: How many squares does a chessboard have?
board-squares.explanation: 8 ranks × 8 files = 64 squares, alternating light and dark.

board-corner.prompt: With the board set up correctly, what color is the square in your bottom-right corner?
board-corner.explanation: Remember "light on the right". If that corner is dark, the board is turned the wrong way.

queen-own-color.prompt: Where does the white queen start?
queen-own-color.explanation: The queen goes on her own color: the white queen on d1 (light), the black queen on d8 (dark).

who-moves-first.prompt: Who makes the first move in a game?
who-moves-first.explanation: White always moves first, then the players take turns.

value-queen.prompt: Roughly how many points is a queen worth?
value-queen.explanation: Rough values: pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. The king is priceless — losing it loses the game.

value-rook.prompt: Roughly how many points is a rook worth?
value-rook.explanation: About 5 points — stronger than a knight or bishop (3) but weaker than a queen (9).

value-minor.prompt: How do a knight and a bishop compare in value?

choices.knight: A knight is worth two bishops

value-minor.explanation: Both are worth about 3. Bishops shine in open positions, knights in closed ones.

knight-jumps.prompt: Which piece can jump over other pieces?
knight-jumps.explanation: Only the knight moves in an L-shape and jumps over pieces.

bishop-color.prompt: Can a bishop move to a square of the other color?

choices.same: No, it always stays on one color

bishop-color.explanation: Bishops only move diagonally, so they stay on the same color all game.

pawn-backward.explanation: Pawns only move forward — think before you push them!

pawn-two-steps.prompt: When may a pawn move two squares at once?

choices.first: Only on that pawn's first move

pawn-two-steps.explanation: Each pawn may move two squares only on its first move, then one square at a time.

kings-adjacent.prompt: Can the two kings stand next to each other?
kings-adjacent.explanation: No. A king would be moving into a square attacked by the other king, which is illegal.

sq-knight-center.prompt: Click every square the knight on e4 can move to.
sq-knight-center.explanation: The knight moves in an L: two squares one way, then one to the side. In the center it has 8 moves.

sq-knight-corner.prompt: Which squares can the knight in the a1 corner reach?
sq-knight-corner.explanation: In the corner it has only 2 moves. As the saying goes: "a knight on the rim is dim".

sq-bishop.prompt: Click every square the bishop on d4 can move to.
sq-bishop.explanation: The bishop moves diagonally any distance, as long as nothing is in the way.

sq-rook.prompt: Click every square the rook on d4 can move to.
sq-rook.explanation: The rook moves along ranks and files any distance if the path is clear.

sq-queen.prompt: Click every square the queen on d4 can move to.
sq-queen.explanation: The queen combines rook and bishop: straight or diagonal, any distance.

sq-king.prompt: Click every square the king on d4 can move to.
sq-king.explanation: The king moves one square in any direction.

sq-pawn-start.prompt: Which squares can the pawn on e2 move to?
sq-pawn-start.explanation: On its first move a pawn may go one square (e3) or two (e4).

sq-pawn-capture.prompt: Which squares can the white pawn on e4 move to?
sq-pawn-capture.explanation: Pawns move straight but capture diagonally. e5 is blocked by the knight, but the pawn can capture on d5 or f5.

sq-escape-check.prompt: The white king is in check. Which squares can it escape to?
sq-escape-check.explanation: The rook on e8 controls the whole e-file, so e2 is still in check. The king must step to the d- or f-file.

mv-castle-short.explanation: Kingside castling: the king moves two squares right (e1 → g1) and the rook jumps to f1. Drag the king to g1.

mv-castle-long.explanation: Queenside castling: the king moves two squares left (e1 → c1) and the rook goes from a1 to d1.

mv-en-passant.prompt: Black just played d7 → d5. Capture en passant!
mv-en-passant.explanation: The e5 pawn captures diagonally to d6, taking the d5 pawn as if it had moved only one square. It must be done right away.

mv-promote.prompt: Promote the pawn to a queen.
mv-promote.explanation: A pawn reaching the last rank becomes a queen, rook, bishop or knight — almost always a queen.

mv-mate-back-rank.explanation: Rd8 is checkmate! Black's own pawns block the king's escape — a back-rank mate.

mv-mate-queen.explanation: Qh8 checks along the 8th rank, and the white king on b6 covers a7 and b7. No escape.

mv-fork.prompt: Find the knight move that attacks both the black king and rook.
mv-fork.explanation: Nc7+ checks the king and attacks the rook on a8 — a fork. Black must save the king and loses the rook.

mv-hanging.prompt: The black queen is undefended. Take it!
mv-hanging.explanation: Rd5 wins the queen for free. Always look for undefended ("hanging") enemy pieces.

mv-escape-check.prompt: The rook is checking your king. Get the king out of check.
mv-escape-check.explanation: The rook controls the first rank, so d1 and f1 are unsafe. Step up to d2 or e2.

castle-in-check.prompt: Which statement about castling is NOT true?

choices.unmoved: The king and rook must not have moved
choices.empty: The squares between them must be empty
choices.inCheck: You may castle while in check
choices.notThrough: The king may not pass through an attacked square

castle-in-check.explanation: You can't castle out of check, through check, or into check.

castle-king-moved.prompt: The king moved and came back to its square. Can it still castle?
castle-king-moved.explanation: Once the king has moved, castling is lost for good — even if it returns.

en-passant-timing.prompt: When can you capture en passant?

choices.immediately: Only on the very next move

en-passant-timing.explanation: Only immediately after the enemy pawn's two-square move. Miss it and the chance is gone.

promotion-pieces.prompt: What can a pawn promote to?
promotion-pieces.explanation: Queen, rook, bishop or knight — never a king. You can have two queens.

stalemate-result.prompt: Black to move is not in check but has no legal moves. What's the result?
stalemate-result.explanation: Stalemate is a draw. When you're winning big, be careful not to stalemate your opponent!

check-meaning.explanation: Check means the king is attacked, and it must be dealt with immediately.

choices.noEscape: The king is in check and cannot escape
choices.noMoves: No moves left but not in check

checkmate-meaning.explanation: Checkmate: the king is in check and can't move away, block or capture the attacker. That side loses.

draw-threefold.prompt: How many times must a position repeat for a draw?
draw-threefold.explanation: The same position three times (same side to move) is a draw.

draw-fifty.prompt: How many moves without a capture or pawn move lead to a draw?
draw-fifty.explanation: The fifty-move rule: 50 moves by each side with no capture and no pawn move.

draw-insufficient.prompt: Which is a draw by insufficient material?
draw-insufficient.explanation: A king and a single bishop cannot checkmate. A queen or rook can.

notation-square.prompt: In the square name "e4", what do the letter and number mean?
notation-square.explanation: The letter (a–h) is the file (column), the number (1–8) is the rank (row).

notation-capture.explanation: "x" means a capture: Nxe5 = knight takes on e5.

notation-check-mate.prompt: Which symbols mean check and checkmate?
notation-check-mate.explanation: "+" is check, "#" is checkmate. "!" praises a good move.

notation-castle.explanation: O-O is kingside castling, O-O-O is queenside castling.

notation-knight.prompt: Which letter stands for the knight in English notation?
notation-knight.explanation: N for kNight, because K is the King. This app shows piece icons (♘), so you don't need the letters.

opening-center.prompt: What should you prioritize in the opening?

choices.center: Control the center (d4, e4, d5, e5)

opening-center.explanation: Central pieces control more squares and can switch to either side quickly.

opening-develop.prompt: Which pieces should you develop first?
opening-develop.explanation: Bring out knights and bishops first. An early queen gets chased around and wastes time.

choices.safety: King safety and connecting the rooks

opening-castle.explanation: Castling takes the king out of the dangerous center and connects the rooks.

tactic-fork.prompt: One piece attacking two enemy pieces at once is called…
tactic-fork.explanation: A fork threatens two targets; the opponent can only save one.

tactic-pin.prompt: A piece can't (or shouldn't) move because it would expose a more valuable piece behind it. That's…
tactic-pin.explanation: A pin: the front piece is stuck because the piece behind is worth more (often the king or queen).

tactic-skewer.prompt: Attacking a valuable piece so that when it moves, the piece behind it falls. That's…
tactic-skewer.explanation: A skewer is a reverse pin: the more valuable piece is in front and must move away.
